title: Lessons From the Agentic Frontier: How the SOC is Winning in the AI Era

segments.text: >> SPEAKER: Please welcome Senior Vice President and
General Manager, Splunk Security, John Morgan.
>> JOHN MORGAN: So, the industry has been modernizing
the security operation center for many years, but it's still
the case that threats are overwhelming our analysts.
Now, we have an opportunity – no, actually, we have an
obligation to stop analyst burnouts and stop threats from
entering into our SOC.
And we're going to think about doing this with AI
and with agents.
This is what we call the agentic SOC.
Yet at the same time, agents are our biggest insider threat.
Now, we see this, we've talked about it, you can look
no further than the exhibit halls, which are now open today.
We cannot the discussion of an agentic SOC unless we, as a
security community, address the fact that these are also
our biggest insider threats.
And by the way, they're also non‑deterministic.
Non‑determinism is a different output even given
the same input.
So, this brings up a key question for us which is,
is this technology a right fit?
How do we think about the security risk in an agentic SOC?
This is the security operation center, our last
line of defense.
Now, we're going to discuss this and what I want to do is
talk about technology and the things that will allow
that to occur.
But at the same time, I want to take a step back and
I want to give you how I personally rationalize this:
how I rationalize the non‑deterministic nature,
how I rationalize the fact that it is a threat in
these certain circumstances.
Then we're going to go through an agentic SOC and
give you some examples of what that looks like.
So, the first issue that I want to talk
about is non‑determinism.
Now, as a community, we grapple, you know, with the
non‑deterministic nature of AI.
And at the same time, you know, we have expectations
of control and how that's actually going
to be predictable.
We know how to engineer things in such a way where the systems
are formulaic with recipes and they're, you know,
a systematic series of controlled events.
But I want to take that step back right now.
Some of the most powerful things in this world are
actually born from a non‑deterministic uncontrolled
set of events.
Alexander Fleming in the 1940s, he was already
a well-known scientist at the time.
But he won a Nobel Prize.
And he won a Nobel Prize because he went on vacation.
He went on vacation, and what he did is he left one of his
petri dishes with Staphylococcus bacteria in it
uncovered during his vacation.
He came back, there was a mold spore that came up through the
ventilation shaft from a completely different and
independent laboratory that was doing something else,
landed in that petri dish.
And that's how we ended up with penicillin.
Now, that's actually changed a lot of people's
lives in medical research.
That's not planned.
That's not determined.
That was definitely not a controlled set of events.
So, the power of unpredictability, it's not
solely related to Gen AI.
Actually, if you think about it, we're building
other things with non‑deterministic features.
Quantum computing.
We're using quantum mechanics and the non‑deterministic state
of qubits in order to create some of the world's
most powerful computers.
Now, there's other things involved, like statistical
probability and distributions, but the bottom line is we're
providing value that we could have never predicted before
using systems that literally have this attribute
of being non‑deterministic.
Now, just like nature has been doing since the dawn of time,
we're at the brink of massive increases in our
capability as we harness the power of the non‑determinism
in our digital systems.
To do things that we couldn't predict.
To say this a little more simply, if you had an outcome
in mind and if you think you had, you know, you knew kind of
the best way to get to that outcome, well, there may be
a better way.
And there may be a better outcome.
And a non‑deterministic system may find it for you.
So, let's touch on the threat.
And I want to think about this in a way, again,
of how I rationalize this within this agentic world.
So, for an organization to compete, we already know we're
going to be embracing AI.
We're going to automate our business decisions,
our coding, and a number of other things.
But at the same time, we know that an agent maybe on a bad
day could express what we think of as malicious intent.
Or it may, even in the best case, make catastrophic
mistakes across your digital infrastructure at,
you know, machine speed.
So, it's kind of the same, you know, with people.
But people don't act as fast.
I would say one of the biggest differences, though,
is that people tend to have a social contract,
at least, most people - not everyone.
But that social contract says that hey, we kind of
understand that our reputation and our credibility is very
important for us if we want to participate in future events.
And we know that AI agents don't have that social contract.
They don't have families to feed.
They don't care about things like prison.
So, how do I rationalize some of this risk?
Again, I'm going to take a step back.
The way I think about it is some of the most simple things,
the most essential things in this world that we
need to live with are also an absolute threat
to our existence.
Think about the air we breathe.
Obviously essential.
But that same air that we breathe, if you're a scuba
diver and you go down deep and you exhibit quite a bit of
pressure and you ascend too fast, it's life‑threatening.
That same air is definitely dangerous if your goal is to
put out a fire that's spreading.
There's many more examples, but the point is essential
things in life are most often also threats.
And AI is entering that realm of essential and a threat.
And what we do, just like we do with everything else,
we have to create the constructs and the processes
to mitigate those threats.
This is where the opportunity comes in with an agentic SOC.
If you harness the power of AI that we just talked about.
But you have to control it.
So, fueled by the volume and the sophistication and the
overall speed of attacks, we have no choice but to automate
and automate more in order to keep up in our
security operation centers.
So, a security operation center contains
a number of things: an open
distributed data platform sort of centered around
tooling and analytics with a collaboration platform where
we've got humans and agents working together,
where the humans are in control and the agents
are making recommendations and sometimes they're taking
complete actions autonomously on our part.
There's also a large data management plane where
we're looking at agent visibility on a massive scale.
Purpose‑built agents are required in order to access
federated data, machine data, and all kinds of information
that has to be ingested in.
Of course, a security operation center wouldn't be
of any value if it didn't have security controls in the
environment as well.
This is your network, your Cloud, your Email,
your identity, your endpoint, and many other controls.
Tight integration for automatic responses.
That's obviously an important component.
But I'd say one of the key ingredients to an agentic SOC,
particularly as you go closer to being autonomous,
is an agentic trust and governance model.
When you put these things together, security teams will
move from being reactive to being proactive at speed
and at scale.
So, for high stakes, we need high visibility and we need a
high efficacy of controls.
The agentic trust and governance model,
this is designed to mitigate those
agentic risks of non‑determinism and behavior.
And it has no standard today.
This is one of the main questions that probably
many of us get asked is:
Hey, I want to deploy agents, what do I need to do?
How do I need to secure it?
I think it's one of the major topics that all of us
are talking about here.
There's many onstage keynotes and others that are looking at
and discussing ideas of what this looks like.
So, I want to give you some of the key things that I see
in what I'm calling an agentic security and governance stack.
It's not everything, but I want to point out some of the
things that I think are different, right?
Using identity as a control plane.
That's not different.
We've got to do it at runtime.
It's probably going to make things like Zero Trust today
look a little soft.
But the thing that is different is at build time
when you design your agents, you need to operate
in something that's called separation of duty.
It's kind of a need-to-know mentality for agents.
And you need to break up a single job into multiple jobs.
And you assign them to different agents so that you
get around, one, the security, and, two,
you can handle things like context windows and memory quite
a bit better that way.
Output validation: There are some things that are similar.
Data leakage prevention, confidentiality.
But it's got to happen at speed and scale
that is different.
But I'd say one key thing is intention.
Because these things are non‑deterministic, how do you
know if that output is hallucinating or if it's just
5 or 10 degrees off?
You need to check that.
On the data side, as companies go from data to
automated business decisions with nothing in between, this is
going to bring a whole new realm of data
security and governance.
Data integrity is going to be paramount.
Who is auditing the data at what time?
It's almost going to look like - we've gone through a number of
things in this industry.
I think this one is going to be data as code.
And we're going to have to manage what we think of as
typical data in this fashion.
Agentic detection and response is another element
in this stack.
I'm not going to go into detail on this.
We hear a lot about it.
This is your MCP servers, your LLMs.
There is a lot of new componentry in the environment.
Not to mention workflows, people's jobs change, processes,
the agents themselves.
They're all fair game for attack surface.
And now things like OpenClaw coming into play.
We have to do it at much more speed and scale,
and we probably have to do it right now.
I'd say one of the very interesting things that is
also changing is compliance.
Not only the new compliance like bias and transparency and
how did your agents come to a particular conclusion,
but even existing compliance like GDPR.
GDPR has things like the right to forget.
But how do you figure out –
now you've got data - in different transformations,
you've got data now in an LLM transform.
You've got data that might have been put into
a vector database.
You've got data that might be in a context window or a KB
cache storing hardware.
All representing this agentic workforce and infrastructure.
But then you've got to make sure that that data is somehow
wiped from all those areas.
So, you've got to be really careful how you do that.
There's other things in this agentic stack and
governance model, like sovereignty, tokenomics.
I won't go through all those but I think this is what,
as an industry, we're trying to figure out right now.
So, I'd like to take a shift and get some practical
examples going here about the agentic SOC.
And to do that, I have a colleague with 25 years
of cybersecurity experience.
And I'd like to welcome onto the stage Fred Frey.
Fred?
>> FRED FREY: Hey, John.
All right.
Thank you, John.
So, RSA is saturated with AI hype.
And yes, while it's well‑founded, I am unfortunately
going to add to that as well.
But I'd like to take a slightly different angle.
I'd like to take a practical angle through examples.
Our first example is set at 3:00 AM.
There's an impossible traveler alert that fires.
One of your employees logged in from New York 20 minutes ago
but now it's found a different IP address,
a different device fingerprint, but the same credentials were
used in Eastern Europe.
You have a junior analyst, Samir.
Samir has only been with your company for a few months.
And he has this impossible task of triaging this detection.
And he has to get it right.
The stakes are too high to mess up.
So, junior analyst.
He has 12 tabs open across five different products, and
he's trying to correlate IP addresses, look at
threat intelligence, look at pattern of life.
And it takes hours, sometimes.
And we don't have hours.
This attacker is in our network and moving laterally
as we speak.
But tonight, let's imagine he has an agentic SOC.
He is not an operator.
He is an orchestrater at this point.
Even though he's a junior analyst, he has the power
and the history of thousands of investigations.
Also, a small army of subject matter experts
who have PhDs in subjects like investigation,
correlation, threat hunting at his fingertips.
Before he even picks up the ticket, the triage has already
provided a full authentication timeline.
Every time this user has logged in and authenticated,
what's their pattern of life for the past 30 days?
Simultaneously, an enrichment agent is checking the Eastern
European IP address against Tor exit nodes, VPNs,
and threat intelligence.
A third correlation and hunt agent is now fanning out and
looking at all of his recent Email logs,
his endpoint telemetry, network proxy events to try and assess
if there's any post-breach activity, or what is this
potential blast radius we're dealing with?
What used to take hours now takes seconds.
Samir is now looking at a dashboard with full context,
and he is very confident in his decision,
much more confident than if he was working on it alone.
No queries.
He didn't have to write any queries.
His subject matter expertise was through the
history of the agents.
It was learned behavior.
But here's where it gets really interesting.
The agent, during the investigation, had flagged
something that Samir wouldn't have caught.
And I posit that maybe even a tier 3 analyst wouldn't have
caught as well.
In this case, the correlation agent had researched a threat
hunt that a senior analyst did with the threat hunting agent
just months ago.
And it identified similar TTPs, stolen credentials.
And what it did in that case is that it added an Email
filter via API using those stolen credentials.
And sure enough, it kicked off a hunt and identified the same
TTP activities here.
One of the superpowers that we really need to harness in
this agentic future is the power of memory.
This tribal knowledge that each SOC has is invaluable.
And it's the one thing you can't give an agent
when it starts.
It has to be learned behavior by watching operators go.
This idea of uplifting a junior analyst to conduct
a threat hunt is really powerful and super exciting.
In an agentic SOC, every investigation makes every
analyst better automatically.
Agents are not just being used reactively.
Agents can prevent issues before they become incidents.
In this next example, I want to talk about
a retail company.
This retail company has a weekly sales report.
They have an automation system, and they're posting
reports to an S3 bucket.
The CFO uses this to track monthly revenue targets.
The customer service team is using this to verify
returns and reports.
And then the business unit, month later, hires a
third‑party analytics partner.
They want to design analytics around buying
patterns, sales trends.
And since all of the data is already there in the S3 bucket,
they've looked, there's no PII data, they say
yeah, let's share this S3 bucket out with our third‑party vendor.
Everything is clean, everything is compliant,
there's no PII.
Few months later, though, drift happens.
The customer support team identifies an innovative idea.
They want the customer Email addresses, home addresses in
this report so that they can build proactive campaigns
to help and support their customers.
It's a legitimate business need.
Developers develop it.
And now we have a problem.
Now, I'm sure everyone in this audience can easily see
the issue while I'm talking about it on stage.
But now we're unintentionally sending PII
data to a third‑party party and we're breaking trust, right?
The trust with our own data policies that can lead to fines,
damages, or worse.
These misconfigurations can lay dormant, and are laying
dormant in many companies right now, for months if
not years, and are hard to identify due to the complexity
of the intent of the flow.
Same scenario now with an AI agent in the loop,
a preventative agent.
This agent understands the code change before
the merge happens.
It understands your infrastructure because you're
using infrastructure as code.
It traces the data flow to the S3 bucket and understands that
S3 bucket and who it's shared with.
It understands your data policies, what you classify
data as from a PII standpoint.
It puts all of these things together and understands that
this merge is going to cause a conflict.
And it proactively blocks the merge before
it becomes an incident.
So, the agentic SOC.
We, as a community, are still in the early days.
We are still converging.
It is very nascent technology and we are
harnessing the power of it.
There is a lot of innovation that's happening really fast.
I'd like to leave you with three ideas.
The first idea, we've already touched on, but I really want
to double-click on: customized agents.
Agents out of the box is not what we need.
We need agents to understand our business practices,
our data, our query structure, our way we
investigate alerts today.
Agents can consume, retain, and recall massive
amounts of data.
And it's critical for them to surface at just
the right time.
This builds trust.
As it's learning our systems and our processes,
we're building trust.
And as John mentioned, AI is a double‑edged sword.
It isn't an all-or-nothing, flip a switch.
Agents need to earn our trust by providing that they have
knowledge of our complicated systems.
Initially, this requires humans in the loop.
But we can't stop there.
We need to quickly move and graduate towards
these systems, towards humans out of the loop
because we just don't scale.
The explosions of agents are unprecedented, and we are just
on the tip of what's about to happen.
Last week at the NVIDIA Conference, Jensen said OpenClaw
is the most successful open-source project ever.
And it's only been out for, like, three months,
enabling anyone with an LLM, API key, and a command shell
to build, maintain, and deploy autonomous agents.
If there is one thing that I've learned throughout history,
when you show me where the customers are entrusting
their data, I'll show you where the hackers are focusing.
It's abundantly clear that the new battleground is AI.
It's equally clear it will be exponentially doubling in the
next couple years.
And this future demands we harness the power of agents to
meet this scale.
With that, I would like to turn it over to John.
>> JOHN MORGAN: Thank you, Fred.
AI agents bring risk.
And non‑determinism can be uncomfortable.
But nature has taught us something important.
Non‑determinism is powerful, and it's a source of innovation.
And with the right trust and governance model,
agentic systems can actually be powerful allies with us.
An agentic SOC provides certainty in a world that's full
of non-predictability at this point.
With threats running at machine speed,
humans are going to need help.
We need agents at our SOC.
But this is not about replacing people.
This is really about empowerment, right?
Empowering people to not just respond, but to start to
predict and be proactive and prevent.
Thank you so much.
